planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped nursery stock in spring in deep, moist, well-drained soil with plenty of room for a large pyramidal crown.

directions: Introduced by Plumtree Nurseries of Nebraska in the late 1920s, Redmond is a selection of American basswood chosen for its dense, uniformly pyramidal habit and straighter, more symmetrical form than seedling trees. Reddish winter twigs and buds add subtle color to the bare canopy, and the fragrant cream-yellow flower clusters in early summer draw bees the same way the straight species does. Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving it room to develop its broad conical crown as a specimen, park, or street tree. It tolerates a range of soils and urban conditions well but appreciates supplemental water during establishment and extended summer dry spells.

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container nursery stock in spring in average, medium-moisture, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade.

directions: Greenspire is by far the most widely planted littleleaf linden cultivar, selected for a strong central leader and dense, uniform, broadly pyramidal habit that makes it an unusually predictable street and boulevard tree. Glossy dark green, heart-shaped leaves turn golden yellow in autumn, and clusters of pale yellow, intensely fragrant flowers open in early to midsummer and draw bees from a considerable distance. Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained soil of average fertility; it is not particular about soil pH and tolerates compaction, heat, and air pollution better than most large shade trees. Its predictable, uniform crown makes it especially useful where a formal allée or matched row of trees is wanted.

planting.note: Plant nursery stock in spring in well-drained, fertile to average loam or clay-loam soil in full sun; Sterling is more heat- and drought-tolerant than most other linden cultivars once established.

directions: Sterling was selected for a strong central leader and a more uniform, broadly pyramidal to oval crown than typical seedling silver lindens, along with a smaller, more garden-appropriate mature size. The dark green leaves have a dense, silvery-white felted underside that flashes brightly whenever the canopy stirs in a breeze, and the fuzzy leaf undersides make this cultivar noticeably more resistant to the aphids and resulting sooty mold that plague other lindens. Fragrant creamy-white flowers open in early to midsummer and are heavily worked by bees. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Sterling handles heat, drought, and urban stress better than most linden selections, making it a strong choice for parking lots and street plantings in warmer parts of its range.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed outdoors in fall for natural warm-then-cold stratification, as Mongolian linden shares the compound seed dormancy typical of the genus and germination can be slow and uneven; container-grown transplants can be set out in spring instead.

directions: The smallest of the cultivated lindens, Mongolian linden forms a neat, pyramidal-to-rounded small tree with distinctive small, dark green, three- to five-lobed leaves quite unlike the plain heart-shaped foliage of other Tilia species, turning a soft yellow in fall. Exfoliating bark on older wood adds winter interest that most lindens lack. Native to north China and the far eastern reaches of Russia, it is exceptionally cold hardy and grows more slowly than the larger linden species, making it a good fit for residential streets, parking areas, and smaller gardens where a full-sized basswood or littleleaf linden would eventually be too large. Plant in full sun to partial shade in alkaline to neutral, loamy, well-drained soil; established trees tolerate urban conditions well.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant nursery stock in spring in deep, moist, well-drained soil; Legend is a more compact, uniform selection of American basswood well suited to street and residential plantings where the straight species would grow too large.

directions: Legend is a patented selection of American basswood chosen for its dense, broadly pyramidal crown, glossy dark green foliage, and notably improved resistance to the leaf rust that commonly disfigures seedling basswoods by late summer. Bright red winter twigs and buds give the bare tree good cold-season color, and the fragrant, bee-attracting cream-yellow flower clusters open in early summer just as in the species. Its smaller, more predictable mature size and vigorous, urban-tolerant growth make it a practical choice for street tree plantings and residential lots too small for a full-sized basswood. Plant in deep, moist, well-drained soil in full sun, and water regularly through the first two seasons to support establishment.
sources: Vermont Community Forestry Tree Selection Tool

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall for warm-then-cold stratification typical of the genus; plant container-grown trees in a sheltered site protected from harsh winter winds and late frosts.

directions: Henry's lime is instantly recognizable among lindens for its long, needle-fine fringed teeth along each leaf margin, a texture unlike any other Tilia in cultivation. New spring growth emerges in bronze and pink-red tones covered in fine silvery star-shaped hairs before settling into soft sea-green summer foliage and yellow-orange fall color. It is also the latest linden to bloom, opening large, richly fragrant flower clusters of fifty to ninety blossoms in late summer when few other trees are flowering. Native to central China and Taiwan, it grows best in a sheltered site with fertile, deep, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, and is a distinctive specimen tree for collectors and larger gardens within its hardiness range.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Transplant in spring into deep, moist, well-drained soil; Ardis grows slowly and can be sited much closer to structures and paths than the towering straight species.

directions: Found as a garden sport by Ardis Sonneman in Vandalia, Illinois, and named in 1970, this is the closest thing to a true dwarf tulip poplar, growing into a dense, slow, rounded small tree only about 12 to 18 feet tall and wide after many years rather than the 70-plus feet of the species. Its leaves are proportionally tiny, only a quarter to a third the size of typical tulip poplar foliage, while the greenish-yellow and orange, cup-shaped flowers remain full-sized and are held at eye level where they can actually be appreciated up close. Plant in deep, moist, well-drained soil in full sun, and give it a spot with room to grow slowly into a rounded specimen; it makes tulip poplar's distinctive foliage and flowers accessible to gardens far too small for the species.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant nursery stock in spring in consistently moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; this selection does not tolerate drought as well as some other shade trees and needs regular water while establishing.

directions: Introduced by J. Frank Schmidt & Son Co., Emerald City was selected for a strong dominant central leader and straighter, more uniformly upright oval habit than the often multi-trunked, wide-spreading straight species, along with deeper glossy green foliage. Its narrower mature footprint makes it far more practical than the species for streetscapes, parking lots, and residential lots where a full-spreading tulip poplar would not fit. It still produces the species' typical yellow-green, orange-centered tulip-shaped flowers in late spring and clear yellow fall color. Plant in full sun in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and irrigate through dry spells, since this selection is less drought-tolerant than many other shade trees.
sources: City of Seattle Trees for Neighborhoods
